claims.claim_text: GPTZero's Hallucination Detector automatically identifies hallucinated sources and poorly supported claims in essays.
claims.evidence_span: GPTZero's Hallucination Detector automatically detects hallucinated sources and poorly supported claims in essays.

claims.claim_text: The citation checker identifies hallucinated references instantly to help educators maintain academic integrity.
claims.evidence_span: Our citation checker identifies these hallucinated references instantly, helping educators maintain academic integrity without spending time on manual verification.

claims.claim_text: GPTZero source finder detects checkable, objective claims in text and matches those to sources from online, academic, and publicly available data.
claims.evidence_span: Source finder will detect as many checkable, objective claims in your text and match those to sources from online, academic, and publicly available data coming from AI-powered search engines.

claims.claim_text: An AI hallucination is a response generated by artificial intelligence that contains false or misleading information presented as fact.
claims.evidence_span: In the field of artificial intelligence (AI), a hallucination or artificial hallucination (also called bullshitting,[1] confabulation,[3] delusion,[4] or mirage[5]) is a response generated by AI that contains false or misleading information presented as fact.[6]

claims.claim_text: Symbolic artificial intelligence models generally do not produce hallucinations, unlike large language models.
claims.evidence_span: Symbolic artificial intelligence models generally do not produce hallucinations, unlike large language models.[12]

claims.claim_text: In computer vision, hallucination was introduced as adding detail to an image to improve it.
claims.evidence_span: In computer vision, since the 2000s, hallucination is adding detail to an image to improve it.

claims.claim_text: AI hallucinations refer to statements made by the system which are either factually incorrect, illogical, or not substantiated by any credible sources.
claims.evidence_span: AI hallucinations refer to statements made by the system which are either factually incorrect, illogical, or not substantiated by any credible sources but sound coherent and fluent on the face of it.

claims.claim_text: The survey aims to provide an extensive overview of current techniques employed to detect, verify, mitigate, or correct hallucinations in generative AI models.
claims.evidence_span: The present survey aims to provide an extensive overview of current techniques employed to detect, verify, mitigate, or correct hallucinations in generative AI models.

claims.claim_text: Datadog built a hallucination detection feature for use cases like retrieval-augmented generation.
claims.evidence_span: In this post, we’ll explore how Datadog built a hallucination detection feature for use cases like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) 3.

claims.claim_text: Faithfulness is the requirement that an LLM-generated answer agrees with the context.
claims.evidence_span: Faithfulness is the requirement that an LLM-generated answer agrees with the context.

claims.claim_text: Breaking down a problem into multiple smaller steps of guided summarization by creating a rubric plays to the strengths of LLMs.
claims.evidence_span: Therefore, if we can break down a problem into multiple smaller steps of guided summarization by creating a rubric, we can play to the strengths of LLMs and then rely on simple deterministic code to parse the LLM output and score the rubric.

claims.claim_text: An AI hallucination occurs when a language model produces content that sounds authoritative and well-reasoned but is factually wrong or entirely made up.
claims.evidence_span: An AI hallucination is when a language model produces content that sounds authoritative and well-reasoned but is factually wrong or entirely made up.

claims.claim_text: Large language models generate text by predicting what words should come next based on patterns in training data.
claims.evidence_span: They generate text by predicting what words should come next based on patterns in training data, not by consulting authoritative sources or verifying facts.

claims.claim_text: Stanford research found that even specialized legal AI tools hallucinate between 17% and 34% of the time.
claims.evidence_span: Stanford research found that even specialized legal AI tools hallucinate between 17% and 34% of the time.
